_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and BC Indigenous nations are using technology on their own terms — for language revitalization, land stewardship, cultural preservation, and self-determined governance. We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘I do not know if the doctor survived’: young mothers recall ‘living hell’ of Nepal’s floods
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Kalpana Nepali was seven months pregnant when the flash floods hit last month, while Pooja Pariyal spent three days on a hospital roof waiting to be rescued. Now, they are living precariously in temporary shelters

For three days, Pooja Pariyal waited on the roof of Trishuli hospital with her three-month-old daughter, Ridhika. On the ground below and around the building, most of her town had been destroyed and churned into a sea of mud in the catastrophic flash floods that surged through the Himayalan border region of Nepal and Tibet in August.

“Those three days were living hell for me, with no food, no working toilet and no one to help with the baby,” she says. “I had nothing to clean my baby’s soiled clothes. My milk supply had reduced because I was hungry and this poor little thing would cry her lungs out.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods

A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her.

Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.

items.title: [Fast Company] Employers have a bizarre new job interview problem: Figuring out if they’re talking to a human
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The recruitment process has become so frustrating lately that more than 1.2 million recruiters and candidates alike take to Reddit each week to peruse a subreddit appropriately called r/recruitinghell.

What’s largely to blame? AI. 

Among U.S. hiring managers, 60% say that artificial intelligence is making it harder to evaluate a candidate’s real skills, according to a report released this week from Western Governors University, a private nonprofit online university based in Utah. Even more alarming is that nearly 20% of the 3,100-plus professionals surveyed cited difficulty confirming whether they are interviewing a human candidate rather than AI, according to the online university’s “Workforce Decoded” report.

“AI is changing more than work; it is changing how employers identify and evaluate talent,” Scott Pulsipher, president of Western Governors University, said in a statement.

Applicants, too, are increasingly frustrated by how companies use AI. Indeed, 44% of candidates view employers’ increased use of AI negatively, citing concerns that qualified applicants may be unfairly screened out, that AI can make mistakes, or that the technology can reduce human interaction, according to an annual report on the state of online recruiting released last week by iHire, an employment platform.

DO DEGREES STILL MATTER?

Many employers are now playing catch-up to find new methods to verify the skills of potential hires, which is especially challenging for entry-level candidates. Among employers who say AI has made it more difficult to evaluate candidate skills, 54% say they’ve cut entry-level hiring, according to the report from Western Governors University.

“When employers cannot trust the signals in front of them, opportunity narrows—especially for people trying to get their first foothold in the workforce,” WGU’s Pulsipher said. 

But employers are increasingly relying on a variety of signals to assess a candidate’s readiness to join the workforce—including degrees, skills, and experience from internships, apprenticeships, or other project-based work. 

AI has already transformed the career trajectories of college graduates with certain degrees, leading to debate about whether this technology is killing the value of a degree in general. But a higher share of employers surveyed this year said they consider college degrees or certificates to be more valuable than they did in 2025—and Pulsipher says that creates an opportunity.

“Higher education and employers have to build a better proof system: credentials that carry meaning, assessments that verify what a person can do, and real-world experiences that show how they think, adapt, and use AI responsibly,” he said.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Office for Future Converts Former School Into Housing for Displaced Families in Ukraine
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Office for Future is converting a former school in Stavyshche, Ukraine, into housing for 42 families displaced by the war. Developed for the Charity Foundation Housing for IDP, the project, titled "Dvir – The Shared Courtyard," reuses the approximately 1,900-square-meter building to create 42 apartments and 200 square meters of shared indoor spaces. The intervention combines the existing structure with new timber elements, an energy retrofit, and the transformation of the former asphalt courtyard into a permeable green space.
